title: Tasks and await
summary: What a Task is, how await gets the value out of it, and why async spreads up the call chain.

steps.title: Waiting without blocking
body: A database query or an API call spends almost all of its time **waiting**: the request is out on the network and your program has nothing to do.

If the code simply stops and waits, its thread is **blocked**. It is held, but doing nothing. A web server that blocks one thread per request runs out of threads. A desktop app that blocks its main thread freezes.

Think of a waiter. A bad waiter takes one order, then stands at the kitchen door until the food is ready. A good waiter hands in the order, gets a ticket, and serves other tables until the kitchen calls.
In C# the ticket is a **`Task`**:
- `Task` is work in progress that will finish at some point.
- `Task<T>` is work in progress that will finish **and produce a `T`**. A `Task<int>` is not an `int`. It is the promise of one.
Methods that return a task are called **asynchronous**. By convention their names end in `Async`: `ReadAllTextAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`, `GetStringAsync`.

steps.prompt: Match each piece to what it means.
pairs: work in progress, with no result value
work in progress that will produce a `decimal`
held by code that is only waiting
a name that tells you the method returns a task

steps.title: async and await
body: **`await`** is how you get the value out of a task.
```csharp
static async Task<int> GetStockAsync(string sku)
await Task.Delay(20);        // stands in for a real database call
return 12;
int stock = await GetStockAsync("TEA");
Console.WriteLine(stock);        // 12
- `await someTask` means: *pause this method here until the task is finished, and let the thread go do other work meanwhile.* When the task finishes, the method carries on from that line.
- `await` **unwraps** the task. Awaiting a `Task<int>` gives you an `int`. Awaiting a plain `Task` gives you nothing; it just waits.
- A method may only use `await` if it is marked **`async`**, and an `async` method returns `Task` or `Task<T>`.
- Inside `async Task<int>` you `return` a plain `int`. The compiler wraps it in the task for you.
`Task.Delay(20)` is a task that finishes after 20 milliseconds. This course uses it as a stand-in for real I/O.
At the top level of a program you can use `await` directly, as in the example.

steps.prompt: Complete the method and the call.
steps.explain: The method produces a string later, so it returns `Task<string>`. `await` pauses until the delay is over. Awaiting the `Task<string>` unwraps it, so `name` is a plain `string`.
With `await` on every call, async code reads top to bottom just like ordinary code. The difference is invisible here: during the 10 ms delay, no thread is blocked.

steps.title: Two warehouse lookups
prompt: The harness provides a fake warehouse database:
```csharp
static class Warehouse
public static Task<int> GetStockAsync(string sku);   // TEA: 12, MUG: 30, POT: 5
Write `static async Task<int> GetTotalStockAsync(string skuA, string skuB)`. It looks up both items and returns their stock added together.
```csharp
await GetTotalStockAsync("TEA", "MUG")   // 42
starter: static async Task<int> GetTotalStockAsync(string skuA, string skuB)
// await Warehouse.GetStockAsync(...) for each sku, then add
solution: static async Task<int> GetTotalStockAsync(string skuA, string skuB)
template: Dojo.Eq("an unknown sku counts as 0", 5, await GetTotalStockAsync("POT", "???"));
Dojo.Eq("the warehouse was asked 6 times in total", 6, Warehouse.Calls);
public static async Task<int> GetStockAsync(string sku)
hints: `Warehouse.GetStockAsync(skuA)` gives you a `Task<int>`. Put `await` in front to get the `int`.
`int a = await Warehouse.GetStockAsync(skuA);` Do the same for `skuB`.
Return `a + b`. The method is `async Task<int>`, so you return a plain `int`.

steps.title: Async all the way
body: Once one method is async, the methods that call it become async too.
```csharp
static async Task<string> LoadNameAsync(int userId) { ... }
static async Task<string> GetGreetingAsync(int userId)
string name = await LoadNameAsync(userId);   // needs await...
return $"Hello, {name}";                      // ...so this method is async too
static async Task ShowGreetingAsync(int userId)   // Task: finishes, but has no result
Console.WriteLine(await GetGreetingAsync(userId));

To use the result you have to `await`. To `await` you have to be `async`. So `async` climbs the call chain until it reaches the top: your top-level statements, a web framework, or a test runner, which all know how to await.
This is normal and expected. It is called **async all the way**. Do not try to stop the chain halfway by forcing the result out of a task; a later lesson shows why that goes wrong.
A method with nothing to return uses `async Task`, the async version of `void`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into an async method that loads a user's name and returns a greeting.
steps.explain: The name has to be awaited before it can be used in the greeting. The method returns a plain `string`; `async` wraps it into the `Task<string>`.

steps.prompt: `GetCountAsync` is declared as `static async Task<int> GetCountAsync()`. What happens with this line?
options: It does not compile: a `Task<int>` cannot be stored in an `int`
It works, and waits for the count
It works, and `count` is `0` until the task finishes
It compiles, but throws an exception when it runs
steps.explain: Without `await` you are holding the ticket, not the meal. The compiler will not turn a `Task<int>` into an `int` for you. Write `int count = await GetCountAsync();`.

steps.title: Finish the chain
prompt: The harness provides `Catalog.GetPriceAsync(string sku)`, which returns a `Task<int>` (TEA costs 5, MUG costs 9).
- `GetPriceWithShippingAsync(sku)` should return the price plus 4 for shipping.
- `DescribeAsync(sku)` should return text like `TEA: 9`.
Someone wrote these as if the calls were ordinary methods. It does not compile. Make the chain async all the way.
template: public static async Task<int> GetPriceAsync(string sku)
hints: The first error: `Catalog.GetPriceAsync(sku)` is a `Task<int>`, not an `int`. It needs `await`.
A method that uses `await` must be marked `async`. Add `async` before `Task<int>` and before `Task<string>`.
Both methods need the same two changes: `async` in the signature and `await` in front of the call.

steps.title: Build an invoice
prompt: The harness provides a fake shop database:
```csharp
record Order(int Id, int CustomerId, int Total);
static class Shop
public static Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int orderId);
public static Task<string> GetCustomerNameAsync(int customerId);
Write two methods:
- `static async Task<string> BuildInvoiceAsync(int orderId)`
Loads the order, then the name of its customer, and returns text like `Invoice 7 for Maya: 120`.
- `static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)`
Builds the invoice for that order and adds it to the `invoices` list. It returns no value.
starter: // 1. load the order   2. load the customer name   3. build the text
static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)
solution: static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)
template: Dojo.Eq("AppendInvoiceAsync adds finished invoices to the list", new List<string> { "Invoice 7 for Maya: 120", "Invoice 9 for Maya: 30" }, invoices);
record Order(int Id, int CustomerId, int Total);
public static async Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int orderId)
public static async Task<string> GetCustomerNameAsync(int customerId)
hints: `Order order = await Shop.GetOrderAsync(orderId);` You need the order first, because the customer id is inside it.
`AppendInvoiceAsync` awaits `BuildInvoiceAsync(orderId)` and calls `invoices.Add(...)` with the result. An `async Task` method needs no `return`.
